reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by ixodid (hard) ticks such as Dermacentor species; despite the name it is most common in the south-eastern and south-central United States rather than the Rocky Mountains
After an incubation of roughly 2-14 days patients develop fever, severe headache, myalgia and malaise, with the classic rash appearing a few days later
The rash is typically maculopapular then petechial and characteristically begins on the wrists and ankles before spreading centripetally to the trunk, often involving the palms and soles
A recalled tick bite is absent in a substantial proportion of cases, so its absence must never be used to exclude the diagnosis
Doxycycline is first-line therapy for all ages, including young children, and should be started empirically on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmatory serology
Delay in starting effective treatment beyond about the fifth day of illness is the strongest predictor of death, making early empirical therapy critical
The core lesion is an infective vasculitis, so laboratory clues include thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and raised transaminases rather than a marked leucocytosis
reference.pathophysiology: Rickettsia rickettsii is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium that, following inoculation by a feeding tick, invades and multiplies within vascular endothelial cells and to a lesser extent smooth muscle of small and medium vessels. Widespread infection of the endothelium produces a systemic small-vessel vasculitis with increased vascular permeability, microvascular leak, oedema, activation of coagulation and localised microthrombi. This vascular injury underlies the rash, the tissue oedema and hypovolaemia, and end-organ damage affecting the brain, lungs, kidneys and other organs, and in severe disease can progress to shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure.
additionalDifferentials: Other spotted fever group rickettsioses and typhus
Human monocytic ehrlichiosis or granulocytic anaplasmosis
Viral exanthems including measles and enteroviral infection
additionalInvestigations: Indirect immunofluorescence antibody serology on paired acute and convalescent sera (the reference confirmatory test, though often negative early)
PCR of whole blood or, preferably, of a skin biopsy of the rash
Immunohistochemical staining of a skin biopsy for rickettsiae
Full blood count and film looking for thrombocytopenia
Serum sodium, renal function and liver enzymes
Coagulation studies where disseminated intravascular coagulation is suspected
redFlags: Altered mental state, meningism or focal neurological signs suggesting meningoencephalitis
Petechial or purpuric rash with hypotension indicating fulminant disease
Respiratory distress or non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
Oliguria and rising creatinine signalling acute kidney injury
Presentation after several days of untreated illness, when mortality rises sharply
reference.prognosis: With prompt doxycycline most patients recover fully, but untreated or late-treated disease carries a high case-fatality rate; survivors of severe illness may be left with neurological deficits or, rarely, limb loss from vascular compromise.
pitfalls: Withholding doxycycline in children over unfounded concerns about dental staining, when short courses are safe and life-saving
Excluding the diagnosis because there is no rash early or no recalled tick exposure
Waiting for serological confirmation before treating, since antibodies are usually undetectable in the first week
Mistaking early non-specific fever for a self-limiting viral illness and discharging without follow-up
Substituting a beta-lactam, which is ineffective against rickettsiae
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
